Elon Musk, the world's richest person, said on Wednesday (Nov 25) that every child in the US will receive two shares in SpaceX, the space and AI company he runs, pledging a gift worth some US$18 billion.

Musk and rival AI company Anthropic have recently laid out sharply different blueprints for sharing some of the spoils of the AI boom, amid growing public and political scrutiny of the industry.

Children will receive one share from the company and one from him personally, Musk said in a brief post on X, without providing details.

In a separate post, Musk said the SpaceX shares will be transferred next month.

"The share directly from me will be transferred when my lockup expires in June next year," Musk added.

SpaceX said earlier on Wednesday it would contribute one newly issued share of its Class A common stock to every currently active Trump Account, adding that Musk will personally match the number of shares donated by the company.

A Trump Account is a program designed to give Americans under the age of 18 a stake in the stock market and help build wealth from an early age. The White House said in October it had opened almost 70 million accounts. SpaceX shares closed at US$127.44 on Wednesday, valuing the pledge at nearly US$18 billion.

SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether Musk's SpaceX share donations would be linked to Trump Accounts.

"What it does is build a massive, long-term retail shareholder base," said Christopher Brankin, global markets advisor at brokerage Mitrade Group. Commentary: New US tariff threat seeks to ramp up pressure on trading partners – will it work?

This strategy of forcing trading partners to the negotiating table may not work as it once did, says Steven Okun from APAC Advisors.

A 3D-printed miniature model depicting U.S. President Donald Trump depicting U.S. flag and word "Tariffs" in this illustration taken, April 17, 2025. REUTERS/Dado Ruvic/Illustration

SINGAPORE: The Trump administration sticks with its America First trade agenda after a shellacking in the US midterms by firing its latest trade salvo on 14 major trading partners, including China, Japan, the European Union and several Southeast Asian countries such as Singapore, Malaysia and Vietnam.

Singapore could be among the hardest hit despite having a free trade agreement (FTA) and running a trade deficit with the US. Under the proposed duties aimed at what Washington terms as excess industrial capacity, Singapore faces a principal tariff rate of up to 20 per cent from the US.

The latest raft of tariffs, announced on Wednesday (Nov 25) and are not due to kick in until January after a period of consultation, ranged from headline rates of 20 per cent to 40 per cent.

But the US Trade Representative (USTR) has given other governments an out with potential lower rates – if they enter or already have an agreement with the US.

This means those with an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (ART) are not impacted – so long as the agreement remains in force. The European Commission, for instance, said in a statement that it expects any measures imposed by the US to respect the 15 per cent ceiling agreed last year, while rejecting US’ claim that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity.

The proposed tariffs are therefore aimed at pushing those which do not have an ART, such as India, Vietnam and Singapore, to sign one.

Singapore 'very disappointed' with proposed US tariffs, says findings fail to account for its economic structure

Asian governments push back, seek deals after Trump’s new tariff salvo

For example, Vietnam faces a capped tariff rate of 20 per cent if it reaches a trade agreement with the US, rising to 35 per cent if negotiations fail. Washington trade insiders expect the Southeast Asian country to sign one on the sidelines of the coming G20 meeting in Miami next month.

India, which remains in talks with the US on a trade deal, would see a 17 per cent tariff rate if an agreement is finalised and a 25 per cent rate if talks fail.

For Singapore, it is 10 per cent with an agreement and 20 per cent without one.

SINGAPORE COULD BE THE HARDEST HIT

Among the 14 trading partners slapped with new tariffs, Singapore stands out as one which has yet to negotiate a trade deal with the US. A 20 per cent rate would also match the Southeast Asian region’s highest rate, presuming Vietnam enters its own ART and similar deals inked by other regional countries remain in force.

“Despite the bilateral FTA and a US trade surplus with Singapore, the Trump administration seems to believe it can extract more and apparently sees little downside risk in trying,” Barbara Weisel of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace told me.

Commentary: Trump’s tariff wall isn’t going anywhere

Snap Insight: US midterms – what an angry ‘lame duck’ president could mean for Asia

There may be other reasons for the USTR’s desire to get Singapore to the negotiating table.

At a recent economic conference organised by the American Chamber of Commerce in Singapore, US Ambassador to Singapore Anjani Sinha said that President Donald Trump requires him to “bring some money” back to the US by increasing Singaporean investment.

Singapore’s foreign direct investment in the United States stands at roughly US$72 billion, making it the third largest in Asia, based on the US Department of Commerce’s data as of 2024. Ambassador Sinha said he expects that number to double.

One will expect the US to require Singapore to announce an increase in FDI if a negotiation happens, as it has done with others.

Singapore has previously said it is taking a cautious approach to any concessions that could secure a lower tariff from the US. In a parliamentary reply in August, Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said the Singapore government must first assess the significant costs and wider trade implications of measures sought by Washington.

It has also persistently denied that its exports to the world’s largest economy are due to some form of excess capacity.

The country's Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry on Thursday morning said it disagrees with the USTR's findings.

WEIGHING THE OPTIONS

Trading partners that do not yet have an ART will have to weigh the actual impact of these potentially higher tariffs versus what they will be required to concede.

Beyond increases in investment commitments, another factor will be what other requirements the US would include, which could relate to trade with China such as those reported to be included in the US negotiations with Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam.

For example, Malaysia agreed to closer cooperation with Washington on export controls, investment screening, transshipment, critical minerals and sensitive technologies – all of which could impact its relations with China. China’s Ministry of Commerce noted last year it had “ serious concerns” regarding parts of the Malaysia-US agreement.

Another ironic twist of these tariffs finds the Trump administration calling foreign governments “unreasonable and unfair” for having their own industrial plans and promoting that their own citizens save money.

An example of the latter is the USTR's mention of Singapore's Central Provident Fund as a policy it deems unreasonable. It had noted that a requirement for citizens to contribute “upwards of 20 per cent of their income” to the programme exceeds that of the US and many developed economies, and that it “promotes savings in a way that depresses consumption”.

In other words, it places tariffs on external governments such as Singapore, for putting their people first.

TARIFFS MAY HAVE A SHORT SHELF-LIFE

The latest trade salvo comes despite US voters making their unhappiness known with the administration’s approach to trade. This should be no surprise though, as Mr Trump's decades-long belief in tariffs will never change.

But the courts have found that the administration often exceeds its authority in issuing them. In February, the US Supreme Court struck down Mr Trump’s so-called “Liberation Day” tariffs. That may again happen here.

The US’ strategy of forcing trading partners to the negotiating table may not work as it once did, given the legal defeats and the likelihood these tariffs may not outlast the administration anyway.

Governments will have to weigh whether to accept a proposed higher rate of tariff under the latest round of “Section 301” probe, which may not last that long, rather than giving up concessions on investment and China-related commitments.

With legal decisions looming and the back half of Trump 2.0 about to start, governments may also reassess how much leverage the US still has.

Steven Okun serves as CEO of APAC Advisors, a geostrategic and responsible investment consultancy based in Singapore. He served as Deputy General Counsel at the US Department of Transportation in the Administration of President Bill Clinton.

Singapore 'very disappointed' with proposed US tariffs, says findings fail to account for its economic structure

The US findings did not take into account the structure of Singapore’s economy, said the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry.

SINGAPORE: Singapore said on Thursday (Nov 26) that it was "very disappointed" with the latest proposed tariffs by the United States over excess industrial capacity and manufacturing.

The Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) on Wednesday proposed a maximum potential tariff rate of 20 per cent, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, on Singapore’s exports to the country after releasing a report on its investigations into the country's acts, policies, and practices related to structural excess capacity and production in specific manufacturing sectors.

"Singapore disagrees with the USTR’s findings and we are very disappointed with the proposed actions against Singapore," said the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry (METI) in a statement on Thursday.

The ministry said the USTR’s findings did not take into account the structure of Singapore’s economy.

"Singapore's global trade surplus is a reflection of our outward- and market-oriented economy as well as our status as a trusted business and trading hub," it said.

"As a small country with limited resources, our priority is to ensure that our markets operate efficiently, and that Singapore remains competitive globally.

The ministry added that Singapore’s economic policies did not protect its domestic market or subsidise manufacturing for export.

"Our free trade agreements seek to lower barriers to trade and investments, and are fully compliant with World Trade Organization (WTO) rules," said METI.

It noted that under the US-Singapore Free Trade Agreement (USSFTA), Singapore levies no tariffs on US exports to Singapore, and the US committed to levying no tariffs on imports from Singapore.

"Since the USSFTA was signed, the US has enjoyed a consistent trade surplus with Singapore for over 20 years," said the ministry.

In 2024, the US’ overall trade surplus with Singapore amounted to US$27 billion and in 2025, this trade surplus grew to US$33 billion, said the ministry.

"Throughout this investigation, the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry has engaged the USTR actively and thoroughly addressed its queries and concerns," said the ministry.

It added that it would be submitting further comments during the upcoming public consultation period to address the issues raised in the report.

The proposed tariff rate could be adjusted to 10 per cent if Singapore reaches a trade agreement with the US, or concludes other negotiations that are responsive to the determinations in this investigation into the acts, policies, and practices of Singapore, according to the USTR report.

METI said it would continue to engage the USTR constructively, including urging it to reconsider its proposed actions on Singapore and to explore ways to reduce the tariff.

The new Miss Universe hails from a Puerto Rican town whose residents have long been known as “the cucumbers”.

Nestled in the mountains of western Puerto Rico, San Sebastián has been celebrating since Jennifer Barreto made history late Tuesday (Nov 24) as the first mother and first married woman to win Miss Universe.

“It was a day for the history books!” exclaimed one municipal worker at the mayor’s office, which was abuzz with excitement.

The town of some 39,000 people – named after its famous karst formations that look like cucumbers – could barely contain itself.

“La Barreto,” as she’s known, was on the lips of many across San Sebastián hours after the win.

“So excited!” said María Rivera as she juggled orders Wednesday morning at El Guayabal bakery. “We were sure she was going to win.”

Miss Puerto Rico's Jennifer Barreto reacts after winning the Miss Universe at the 75th Miss Universe pageant in San Juan, Puerto Rico, Tuesday, Nov 24, 2026. (AP Photo/Alejandro Granadillo)

Barreto, 27, has one daughter and two master’s degrees, in research psychology and clinical social work. She also works as a prevention specialist with the US Department of Defense, developing strategies to combat harmful behaviours.

Cardona attended the pageant, while fans gathered in San Sebastián’s public plaza to watch on a big screen. Afterward, they formed a caravan, honking their horns into the night to celebrate Barreto’s victory.

Asian governments push back, seek deals after Trump’s new tariff salvo

Singapore says it is “very disappointed”, Japan calls the proposed duties “regrettable”, while other economies are looking to existing or ongoing trade negotiations to limit the impact.

File photo. A container ship is seen near the Hai Phong International Container Terminal in Vietnam, Apr 16, 2025. (Photo: Reuters/Athit Perawongmetha)

SINGAPORE: Asian trading partners pushed back against US President Donald Trump’s latest tariff salvo on Thursday (Nov 26), with Singapore saying it was “very disappointed” by the proposed duties and Japan calling the move “regrettable”.

South Korea said it would hold further talks with Washington to safeguard its interests, while Vietnam sought to quickly conclude a trade deal and Taiwan expressed confidence its previously agreed 15 per cent tariff rate would hold.

China and India have also rejected Washington’s claims over excess industrial capacity.

The responses came after the Trump administration proposed new tariffs on 14 major trading partners, including some of Asia’s biggest economies and manufacturing hubs.

The US Trade Representative (USTR) proposed headline tariff rates of between 20 per cent and 40 per cent to counter what Washington described as excess industrial capacity and other market-distorting practices that undermine US manufacturing.

But the actual duties could be capped at lower rates under trade agreements already concluded or still being negotiated with Washington.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the tariffs would not take effect until after a Jan 25 public hearing.

SINGAPORE "VERY DISAPPOINTED"

Singapore said it disagreed with the USTR’s findings and was “very disappointed” with the proposed actions.

The Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry (METI) said the findings did not take into account the structure of Singapore’s outward- and market-oriented economy.

“Singapore’s economic policies do not protect our domestic market or subsidise manufacturing for export,” the ministry said.

METI said it had actively engaged the USTR throughout the investigation and “thoroughly addressed its queries and concerns”.

Singapore will submit further comments during the upcoming public consultation period and continue engaging Washington, including urging the USTR to reconsider its proposed measures and exploring ways to reduce the tariff.

The USTR has proposed tariffs of up to 20 per cent on Singapore goods, with exemptions for certain products.

CHINA REJECTS "OVERCAPACITY" AS POLITICAL PRETEXT

China rejected Washington’s allegation that it was a source of excess industrial capacity, but stopped short of threatening retaliation.

“The so-called issue of ‘industrial overcapacity’ does not really exist and should not be used as a pretext for political manipulation,” a spokesperson for China’s embassy in Washington said.

The spokesperson urged both sides to jointly deliver on agreements reached between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Under the excess factory capacity probe, USTR said China would face the highest capped rate of 20 per cent, which would be added to duties of roughly 25 per cent imposed during Trump's first term.

That rate would comply with a US-China trade truce that expires on Jan 10. But if the truce unravels, China's rate would rise to 40 per cent, the USTR said.

JAPAN CALLS TARIFF PROPOSAL ‘REGRETTABLE’

Japan on Thursday called Washington’s proposed tariffs “regrettable” and rejected the US assertion that it had structural excess manufacturing capacity.

"Japan does not have any non-market policy practices or structural excess production capacity," said Japan's top government spokesman Minoru Kihara.

"It is regrettable that a proposed measure targeting Japan has been announced in spite of this."

Trump announces new tariffs on 14 trading partners including China and Singapore

VIETNAM PUSHES FOR TRADE DEAL

Vietnam said it was working to finalise a trade deal with the United States, vowed to act on "overcapacity" and to tighten forced labour regulations in an effort to avoid Washington's proposed new tariffs.

The ministry said it would participate fully in the next stages of the USTR investigation, including registering for and attending the public hearing, presenting its views and responding to questions from US officials.

The US is Vietnam's largest export market; the US' trade deficit with Vietnam is the largest that it has with any partner.

Vietnam has yet to conclude its trade negotiations with Washington.

Under the USTR proposal, Vietnamese goods would face a capped tariff rate of 20 per cent if an agreement is reached. The rate could rise to 35 per cent if negotiations fail.

Vietnam said it had made commitments under a framework trade agreement in October 2025 and made reforms to address US concerns.

"At the same time, efforts will be made to prevent the risk of overcapacity, curb illegal circumvention and transshipment, combat origin fraud, and effectively enforce regulations prohibiting the import of goods produced using forced labour," it said.

Vietnam and the US meanwhile "are working toward finalising negotiations for a reciprocal, fair, and balanced trade agreement as soon as possible".

Taken together, "these factors will serve as a crucial basis for the United States to consider applying a tariff rate lower than the maximum level proposed in the preliminary findings".

INDIA REJECTS EXCESS CAPACITY CLAIM

India said on Wednesday it was examining the USTR notice and reiterated that it did not have structural excess capacity in any sector.

New Delhi said it had engaged constructively throughout the US investigation and argued that trade-related concerns should be addressed through its ongoing negotiations with Washington for a bilateral trade agreement.

“India remains committed to working closely with the United States towards the early conclusion” of the agreement, its trade ministry said.

Under the latest US proposal, Indian imports would face tariffs of up to 25 per cent, but Greer said the rate would be capped at 17 per cent if the two sides strike a trade deal.

New Delhi and Washington agreed to a framework for a trade deal in February, which brought down a punitive tariff on most Indian goods from 50 per cent to 18 per cent. The higher rate had been imposed in August 2025 after an earlier round of negotiations collapsed.

Subsequently, the Supreme Court invalidated Trump's use of emergency powers to impose sweeping tariffs globally, leading to a 10 per cent baseline rate.

But a final trade deal between two of the world's biggest economies remains elusive.

Washington has cited India’s industrial expansion policies, inadequate labour protections, market access barriers and failure to address global excess capacity among practices it says disadvantage US producers.

TAIWAN CONFIDENT 15% RATE WILL HOLD

Taiwan said it was confident Washington would maintain the 15 per cent tariff rate previously agreed between the two sides.

Taiwan and the US signed an investment cooperation memorandum of understanding in January and an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade in February.

Those arrangements secured preferential treatment for semiconductors and other technology products, which account for more than 70 per cent of Taiwan's exports to the US.

Based on communications between Taipei and Washington, Taiwan's government said it is confident that both sides will maintain the previously agreed-upon 15 per cent.

"The US has one main goal, which is to rebuild the legal basis for its reciprocal tariff policy. It is not to change the content of the agreements themselves," Taiwan Vice Premier Cheng Li-chiun, who has led trade talks with Washington, told reporters.

"Both sides have repeatedly said they hope to maintain the content of the agreements. So the agreement as a whole will not change and will not be renegotiated," she added.

Separate Section 232 tariffs on semiconductors and their derivatives have not yet been announced, but Taiwan has already secured most-favoured treatment in advance through the MOU, Cheng said.

Taiwan is home to TSMC, the world's largest contract chipmaker, which is investing US$265 billion to build new factories in the US.

Under January's deal with the US, Taiwanese companies will invest US$250 billion to boost production of semiconductors, energy and artificial intelligence in the US, while Taiwan will also guarantee an additional US$250 billion in credit to facilitate further investment.

Taiwan is also investing US$4.4 billion in a new liquefied natural gas project in Alaska that Trump has championed, though details remain to be ironed out.

Commentary: Trump’s tariff wall isn’t going anywhere

Commentary: Middle powers need the US – when it comes to China exports

SOUTH KOREA SEEKS FURTHER TALKS

South Korea said it would hold further consultations with Washington to safeguard its national interests, while arguing that its manufacturing sector was an integral part of US supply chains.

Seoul’s Industry Ministry said it had stressed during consultations before the announcement that the issue of excess industrial capacity did not apply to South Korea.

The USTR proposed a capped tariff rate of 15 per cent on South Korean goods, including existing most-favoured-nation duties.

However, the rate could rise to 25 per cent depending on the outcome of follow-up consultations and progress in implementing existing trade agreements.

South Korea and the US reached a trade agreement last year to lower tariffs on South Korean exports from 25 per cent in exchange for a combined US$350 billion investment package.

THAILAND SAYS RATE IN LINE WITH EARLIER TALKS

Thailand said Washington’s proposed tariff of up to 18 per cent on Thai goods was in line with previous negotiations between the two sides.

The commerce ministry said the proposed rate would help Thai products remain competitive in the US, Thailand’s biggest export market.

items.title: France's political mainstream risks presidential vote debacle with no clear candidate
items.summary: Hard-right and hard-left candidates dominate the polls ahead of next year's presidential election.
items.body:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images

Image caption,

Protests on the streets of France over students' concerns and the cost of living have been marked by looting and unrest in recent weeks

ByHugh Schofield

Paris correspondent

France's political mainstream faces wipe-out at the presidential election in April-May 2027, unless it acts fast to choose who it wishes to stand.

With every poll confirming the dominance of hard-right and hard-left leaders Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon, candidates of the middle-ground – the old "legacy" parties – are being squeezed out of the game.

In theory any contender from centre-right or centre-left who was chosen in the first multi-candidate round of voting in April should be in a strong position to win in the play-off a fortnight later.

That is because at their separate ends of the spectrum both Le Pen and Mélenchon have more people who oppose than support them.

But personal rivalries, lack of preparation and differing political visions have so far put paid to any hope of a meaningful challenge.

"The game in the centre is totally blocked," says political writer François Fressoz at the left-leaning Le Monde newspaper. "The partisans of reason have lost their reason."

On the left – the old Socialist Party and its acolytes – there is at least agreement on a candidate: European Parliament MP Raphaël Glucksmann.

His problem is that allies who he might once have counted on – Greens, Communists and other small left-wing parties, not to mention many Socialist voters – are being pulled inexorably into the Mélenchon orbit.

Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images

Image caption,

The protests started as an expression of anger at conditions in high schools

In the last two weeks, Green party leader Marine Tondelier, a majority of Communist parliamentary deputies and one-time Socialist presidential hopeful Benoît Hamon have all thrown in their lot with the leader of France Unbowed (LFI).

Another prominent figure of the left – François Ruffin – has also withdrawn from the race, bowing to the unbowed Mélenchon's now almost total command of the field.

So with the soft-left emasculated, the main hope for an alternative to Le Pen and Mélenchon has to be focused on the right. But here the prospects – which until recently seemed bright – are now clouded with gloom.

"A Mélenchon–Le Pen duel in round two is not yet inevitable," says Guillaume Tabard, political analyst at the conservative Le Figaro newspaper. "But it is looking increasingly probable."

In recent weeks the poll ratings of the main centre-right hopeful Edouard Philippe – a former prime minister under President Macron – have fallen sharply, and he is now consistently placed behind Mélenchon in the first round of the vote. Marine Le Pen is way ahead of both.

Other candidates for command of this centre-right "space" are circling. They include another former Macron prime minister, Gabriel Attal; the leader of the right-wing Republicans (and former Macron interior minister), Bruno Retailleau; and now – a surprise new challenger – the mayor of Cannes, David Lisnard.

Image source, AFP via Getty Images

Image caption,

David Lisnard (centre) has seen membership of his micro-party Nouvelle Energie jump to more than 100,000

Lisnard, who stands on a liberal economic platform of less state and lower taxes, has emerged from nowhere to become the man of the hour. Membership of his micro-party Nouvelle Energie (New Energy) has shot up to more than 100,000, and he is being taken seriously as a possible Philippe replacement.

But this very multiplicity of names – not to mention others like judoka Teddy Riner, journalist Natacha Polony and former prime minister Dominique de Villepin – betrays the essential weakness of the centre-right challenge.

According to veteran commentator Nicolas Baverez, "If you want to win an election, it's quite simple: you need a strategy, a programme, and activists. Right now in the space between Le Pen and Mélenchon we have none of that: there is a total vacuum.

"The most glaring absence is digital. Mélenchon especially, but Le Pen too, are running extremely effective social media campaigns. In the middle… nothing."

Guillaume Tabard agrees that the lack of a shared platform is proving a serious handicap.

"In recent weeks we have seen Marine Le Pen issue her manifesto proposals for reforming pensions. We have seen Jean-Luc Mélenchon publish his programme in a best-selling book," he says.

items.title: Has global jihadism failed, or is it simply changing shape?
items.summary: Jihadist groups appear to be focusing on local issues rather than global terror. Does it signify a real change?
items.body:
ByMina al-Lami

Chief jihadist media specialist, BBC Monitoring

Rice, pasta, sugar, cooking oil and beans are hardly what you'd expect to see in jihadist propaganda. Yet these were among the supplies that al-Qaeda's Somali branch, al-Shabab, said its "charity" had handed out to hundreds of struggling families in August, as it publicised the aid through its social media accounts and radio station.

The group, which controls large parts of rural southern and central Somalia, has been keen to show off its so-called humanitarian work throughout 2026.

"May God reward them," said a local woman in one of al-Shabab's videos.

It's all part of an effort to win over local communities and present itself as more than just a jihadist group.

Image source, Telegram

Image caption,

Al-Shabab has been publicising its humanitarian work

A quarter of a century after al-Qaeda's 9/11 attacks in the US, and 12 years after Islamic State group (IS) declared its so-called caliphate in Iraq and Syria, the jihadist movement looks very different.

Rather than focusing on attacking the West or fighting for a global Islamic state, some - especially those linked to al-Qaeda - are putting more effort into winning power closer to home. And they seem increasingly willing to make compromises along the way.

Because of this, a debate is growing within the movement. While hardliners reject compromise, pragmatists see working with local groups and former enemies as a way to gain power. But do the pragmatists represent a genuine change or simply a shift in tactics to achieve the same ultimate goals: establishing a state that applies their strict interpretation of Islamic Sharia law both at home and in its dealings with the outside world?

Significant defeats

Neither al-Qaeda nor IS has achieved its ultimate dream: taking over one or more countries and ruling them according to their strict interpretation of Islam.

Both have suffered major defeats, lost leaders and faced years of international pressure. IS, which once controlled vast areas of Iraq and Syria, lost its last territorial stronghold in 2019. But jihadism hasn't gone away.

Africa is now the main battleground for jihadism, with al-Qaeda's powerful branches, JNIM in the Sahel (Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger) and al-Shabab in Somalia, fighting long-running insurgencies. IS, its bitter rival, has active branches in Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of Congo, the Sahel, Mozambique and Somalia.

One major source of inspiration, and envy, whether jihadists admit it or not, is Syria's new president, Ahmed al-Sharaa. The former IS and then al-Qaeda commander was once wanted by the US but rose to power in Syria in December 2024 and was welcomed by Western leaders.

Once known by his militant nom de guerre Abu Mohammed al-Jolani, he led the jihadist group Nusra Front - initially linked to IS and then al-Qaeda - and later the group Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS).

He gradually broke ties with both IS and al-Qaeda and distanced himself from their calls for global jihad.

Instead, he focused on Syria, building a local power base in the north-western Idlib province.

What surprised everyone was his growing willingness to work with non-Islamist groups and engage with foreign powers. As HTS advanced on Damascus, its leadership sought to reassure the international community, reaching out even to Russia, a key ally of then-president Bashar al-Assad, to allay fears of an Islamist takeover.

That pragmatism, combined with favourable geopolitical conditions - including a weaker Russia and Iran - helped him take power in Syria.

But the sight of him being welcomed by world leaders, including US President Donald Trump, was even more remarkable.

Image source, AP

Image caption,

Trump joked with Sharaa when he visited the White House

During Sharaa's visit to the White House in November 2025, Trump sprayed him with his own branded cologne, jokingly asked how many wives he had and praised him as a "very strong leader".

For some jihadists, Sharaa's success has been inspiring. Others, however, see his actions as a betrayal of everything they believe in.

IS has declared jihad against Syria's new Islamist government, branding Sharaa and his officials "apostates", and has carried out attacks against government forces on that basis. Other hardline clerics have taken a similar stance, but have stopped short of openly calling for jihad against Sharaa.

The divide between hardline jihadists and their more pragmatic counterparts has fuelled a bitter online debate since 2025, with rival voices trading accusations of betrayal and even publishing competing books to defend their positions.

Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

Sharaa, centre, in 2016, was once a jihadist leader wanted by the FBI

For hardliners, going too far can mean abandoning their core beliefs. This might include holding back from imposing their strict version of Islamic law, accepting "man-made" laws or a constitution, taking part in elections, working with non-Islamist groups, or building ties with governments they consider "infidel".

Another source of inspiration for jihadists was the Taliban's return to power in Afghanistan in 2021, as it showed that an Islamist movement could eventually take control of a country after years of fighting Western-backed forces. It engaged local groups, slowly secured power across the country, used international diplomacy, and bided its time before taking the capital, Kabul, in a lightning offensive.

A means to an end?

Two groups are especially worth watching: al-Qaeda's branches in Mali and Somalia.

In late April, al-Qaeda's Sahel branch, known as JNIM, showed considerable pragmatism by joining forces with nationalist Tuareg separatists - whom it had occasionally fought - to launch a major offensive that threatened Mali's military rulers. It even went as far as to call the Tuaregs "brothers".

But it's not just JNIM's growing military strength that's attracting attention. It's also how the group is presenting itself.

Its propaganda once prominently featured al-Qaeda's leaders, slogans and calls for global jihad. Since late 2024, however, its videos have dropped the familiar al-Qaeda branding.

And instead of talking about global Muslim causes, JNIM has increasingly focused on local problems, portraying itself as a defender of ordinary people against corrupt and abusive rulers.

It has repeatedly accused Mali's military government and its Russian allies of killing civilians and making people's lives worse.

In April, it appealed to "all sincere patriots" to help build a "new Mali", promising security, justice and prosperity alongside Islamic law.

It has even suggested it could have "balanced relations" with Russia, despite the fact they're fighting Russian forces backing Mali's government. Its wording echoed that of HTS to Russia as it advanced on Damascus.

There are parallels with Sharaa's approach in Syria: build local alliances, reassure potential enemies and avoid giving outside powers a reason to intervene.

Africa security specialist Aman Bezreh sees similarities between the two groups, but says JNIM's shift may take time.

"JNIM has indeed shown signs of pragmatism similar to HTS", she says. "However, its rebranding has progressed more slowly because the group is simultaneously focused on expanding into new territories and recruiting from diverse pools."

Taliban v Sharaa

The debate over which path to follow is also taking place within JNIM's leadership, according to Wassim Nasr, a France 24 journalist and jihadism expert.

He says one camp favours the Taliban's approach of taking power through force with minimal concessions. The other, which he says currently has the upper hand, favours an approach closer to that of Syria's HTS - making compromises and building wider alliances to gain power more quickly.

Nasr believes JNIM may borrow from both models, but that a break with al-Qaeda is inevitable as a result of its political evolution.

Like JNIM, al-Shabab in Somalia appears willing to make deals with former enemies.

According to Abdullahi Guji, BBC Monitoring's Somalia specialist, al-Shabab reached a truce in October with a powerful Somali tribe, the Ma'awisley, whose fighters had been at the forefront of the fight against the group.

The tribe has since withdrawn its fighters from the front line, dealing a serious blow to the government's campaign against jihadists, says Guji.

Guji believes the group may soon have a chance to test whether it can seize power and establish itself as an alternative government across wider parts of the country.

African Union forces are withdrawing from Somalia amid funding cuts and the approaching end of their mandate in December. Meanwhile, the Somali government is facing political crises and rebellions, creating vulnerabilities al-Shabab could exploit, he adds.

There's another reason some jihadists may see an opportunity to expand: they believe Western governments have bigger fish to fry.

With the war in Ukraine, US-Iran conflict in the Middle East and growing rivalries with China and Russia, fighting jihadists is no longer the priority it was after 9/11.

The US withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021 and the Taliban's return to power, followed by Sharaa's rise in Syria, have reinforced that belief.

Image source, EPA

Image caption,

The Taliban has inspired many jihadists

Colin Clarke, executive director of the Soufan Center, a non-profit research group that focuses on security, says some jihadist groups have learnt that avoiding confrontation with the US can help them escape Western military action and "live to fight another day".

That doesn't mean the West has stopped fighting terrorism. But if jihadists believe it is distracted or less willing to intervene, they may feel emboldened to pursue power.

History lessons

Unlike its fiercely uncompromising rival IS, al-Qaeda has long shown some flexibility in pursuing its goals. But history offers a warning.

After the 2011 Arab uprisings, which largely sidelined al-Qaeda, affiliated jihadist groups in Yemen, Libya and Tunisia began using the name Ansar al-Sharia (Supporters of Sharia) to win local support without carrying the al-Qaeda brand.

In Mali in 2012, al-Qaeda leaders advised jihadists who had seized the north alongside Tuareg separatists not to rush into imposing strict Islamic rules. Instead, they urged them to work with local allies, avoid alienating communities and play down their al-Qaeda links.

The message wasn't to give up their ambitions. It was to show strategic patience until the time was right. That same thinking could be at work today.

More from InDepth

• Democrats have an identity crisis - it won't be an easy fixPublished30 October

• Russia's mega-rich are already imagining a future after PutinPublished16 November

• Europe's youth is on the march - but does anything actually unite them?Published29 October

So are these groups really changing their ambitions, or just their tactics? Even those advocating compromise aren't necessarily abandoning their dream of establishing a state ruled by their strict interpretation of Islamic law.

Clarke wonders whether this more pragmatic approach could be a "Trojan horse strategy" – a way for jihadist groups to gain power without giving up their longer-term goals.

"The big question is whether being in power actually moderates these groups, or whether they're simply changing their tactics to survive and strengthen their position," he says.

But not everyone is changing tactics.

IS remains firmly committed to its global ambitions and rejects compromise. Al-Qaeda's Yemen branch, AQAP, continues to call for attacks against the US and Israel, and urges "lone wolf" attacks against Western and Jewish targets.

And it's too early to say whether groups like JNIM and al-Shabab will follow the Taliban or Syrian examples, and whether they're willing to make compromises.

Some jihadist groups may become more focused on local politics as they face the challenges of governing. Others may simply be hiding their wider ambitions until they're strong enough to pursue them.

The global jihadist dream may have failed, but jihadism is far from finished.

In Mali in 2012, al-Qaeda leaders advised jihadists who had seized the north alongside Tuareg separatists not to rush into imposing strict Islamic rules. Instead, they urged them to work with local allies, avoid alienating communities and play down their al-Qaeda links.
The message wasn't to give up their ambitions. It was to show strategic patience until the time was right. That same thinking could be at work today.

items.title: A renovation was meant to improve these Hong Kong homes - it ended in a blaze that killed 168
items.summary: A year after one of Hong Kong's deadliest fires, families left behind are still waiting for justice.
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

The fire was one of Hong Kong's deadliest in decades

ByGrace Tsoi, BBC World Service, Phoebe Kong, BBC Chinese , Reporting fromHong Kong and Yvette Tan

It was a sunny Wednesday afternoon on 26 November last year, and Mrs Lau was attending a dance class at an activity centre close to her home.

At around 14:45 she heard the faint sounds of fire engine sirens - but didn't think much of it.

It was only a while later, when she started receiving calls from a friend, that she found out that Wang Fuk Court - the eight-block apartment complex she had called home for the past 40 years - was ablaze. And her husband - a wheelchair user - was trapped inside their home.

"I grabbed my things quickly and ran down without even putting my shoes on properly," Mrs Lau, who wanted to be identified only by her surname, told the BBC.

When she got there, the building had been cordoned off by police.

She called her 74-year-old husband but he told her not to worry - he hadn't heard an alarm so it was probably a small fire, he said.

Mrs Lau could only watch helplessly as the blaze tore through Wang Fuk Court at a peak speed of about 10m (33ft) per second - an "unprecedented" rate, a final report released by an independent committee in relation to the deadly blaze that killed 168 people found.

It was a tragedy that was entirely preventable but happened as a result of a series of human errors, fire safety failures, alleged fraud and suspected corruption, said the report.

Image source, Supplied

Image caption,

Lau Man Kwong took care of his grandson before his death (blurred at source)

"It was ferocious… I saw the fire jump [from one building to another] - then a huge fireball burst. It was truly hell on Earth. How could anyone possibly escape?" said Mrs Lau.

She tried calling her husband again. This time, there was no answer.

The body of Lau Man Kwong was eventually found by rescuers - he had locked himself inside the toilet.

"He was wearing his slippers, sitting on the toilet and clutching his identity card," said his wife, who added that she escaped death "by the narrowest margin".

"I would have held onto my husband and died with him.

"He was such a good person. I just don't understand why he had to die in such a terrible way."

Mr Lau and his wife moved into Wang Fuk Court in 1983 - the year the building was completed.

She recalls an idyllic life - a family with three children who were able to grow up close to the sea and spend weekends playing at a nearby park.

"All three of my children adored my husband… He could be very stern, and I was the only woman who could make him laugh."

No way out

In 2024, mandated renovations began in Wang Fuk Court.

In Hong Kong, all buildings over 30 years old have to undergo an inspection - and any necessary renovations as a result.

Like many building complexes in Hong Kong, Wang Fuk Court had a management committee that oversaw things like building repairs. As many as 57 construction companies submitted bids. But the company that won, Prestige Construction and Engineering (PC&E), submitted the most expensive bid at HK$336m ($42.8m; £32.4m).

Residents, many of whom were over 65, had to bear the cost. The hefty bills triggered protests but eventually, the contract was signed. But once the renovations began in July 2024, residents were unhappy.

Among the complaints was that workers constantly smoked on site, dropping cigarette butts everywhere.

The 1,154 page report suggested the fire was caused by a lit cigarette.

Figure caption,

Watch: Christy says she still sends WhatsApp messages to her husband who died in the blaze

There were also complaints about most of Wang Fuk Court's eight buildings having their windows taped over with foam boards to stop debris falling in - blocking daylight or any sort of view at all, for months.

All eight buildings were also covered in a protective mesh netting and bamboo scaffolding.

The report also found that after typhoons damaged the original scaffolding nets in 2025, cheaper non-fire-retardant replacements were chosen - something that was done as a "cost-saving measure at the expense of the safety of the residents".

Residents had filed nearly 140 complaints to six government departments, including the fire services and the buildings departments, in and after 2024, but these were largely ignored, the report went on to say.

It also revealed that a staff member of the estate's property manager, ISS, had turned off the power supply to the fire alarms in all eight buildings - which is why no alarms rang on the day itself.

ISS later told the BBC it had "reviewed and reinforced its procedures [and] staff training" in Hong Kong, adding that it takes the findings of the report "very seriously".

But for those who did manage to flee their homes - the emergency staircase turned out to be another death trap. Windows were removed from some fire escape stairwells to create temporary openings for workers - letting in smoke and cutting off vital escape routes.

Dozens, including Christy's husband, died in such stairwells.

Image source, Lam Yik / BBC Chinese

Image caption,

Christy's daughter celebrated her ninth birthday the day before the fire

Christy, who wanted to be identified only by her first name, says her husband was at home alone when the fire broke out. She only found out about it when her friends sent her messages about it. By the time she made it to the apartment complex, it was already cordoned off.

She found out later that he had died of smoke inhalation in the stairwell, something she says that is at least of some consolation to her.

"My husband's body would have been burnt and he would have been in more pain if he was at home. At the very least… his suffering was minimal."

Christy says her family had just celebrated their eldest child's ninth birthday the day before - they had saved some leftover cake in the fridge to eat the next day. Their father never got to eat it.

Both children have been deeply affected by the loss of their father.

Her youngest child, a seven-year-old boy, had "covered his ears and yelled" when he was first told what had happened to his father.

He now often comforts his mother, saying he will take care of her as he is the only man in the family.

"He hides his emotions. A seven-year-old child should not behave this way, and I feel heartbroken," says Christy, who has herself been diagnosed with PTSD and depression.

Her daughter has "extreme thoughts" she says, and channels her emotions through art.

She turned 10 on Wednesday, but this year, there was no birthday celebration in sight.

Her birthday, she says, will now instead be a day to commemorate her father.

Bid-rigging and rubber stamps

Wang Fuk Court's problems date back to before the renovations began.

The management company hired to oversee and supervise the project, Will Power, conspired with PC&E to defraud residents in Wang Fuk Court, according to the city's Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC).

Although PC&E was found to have breached safety requirements and violated building department rules for multiple previous projects, homeowners at Wang Fuk Court were told that they had a clean record.

The ICAC alleges that this was part of a lucrative scheme, with Will Power's director Wong Hap-yin, along with other individuals, laundering over $5m in suspected proceeds from the tendering process from Wang Fuk Court, among other housing projects.

Once PC&E cinched the contract, Will Power's registered inspector - an individual meant to oversee the renovations - merely rubber-stamped the documents, without having actually conducted any inspections personally, the report added.

Will Power has been since liquidated and PC&E could not be reached for a response.

Both companies - Will Power and PC&E - and seven individuals have been charged with 25 counts of offences including including manslaughter, conspiracy to defraud, attempting to pervert the course of public justice and tax evasion.

Four of them are still in custody but none of the cases have gone to trial yet.

The report said both companies involved were the "main culprits responsible".

But it also directed heavy criticism at authorities, saying that "no government department took effective ownership of various fire safety issues and complaints about fire hazards fell into a vacuum".

One expert, Prof John Burns of Hong Kong University, had called the event the "largest governance crisis" that authorities have faced since 2020 - a reference to the controversial National Security Law that was passed in that year.

On the day the report was released, almost one year after the fire, Hong Kong's housing chief Winnie Ho resigned and the city's top leader John Lee apologised for the first time, promising that a "large number" of reforms would be rolled out.

Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

Homeowners at Wang Fuk Court (pictured) were told their construction company had a clean record

A shell of a home

Five months after the fire, Mrs Lau was allowed into her flat for the first time to collect any personal belongings that might have remained.

In her first visit, she was given just three hours to retrieve 40 years' worth of belongings.

Pictures taken from the visit show a home that has been utterly burned out - with every surface blackened and soot covering the floor.

"I almost fainted when I saw what had become of my home. I don't understand how the home I had built, such a warm and beautiful home, could end up like this," said Mrs Lau.

Image source, Supplied

Image caption,

The frame of Mr Lau's wheelchair was one of the few things left in their burnt home

Her children, who came with her, described the house as a "war zone". Among the rubble, they found broken pieces of a piggy bank that Mr Lau had dutifully filled with coins every day for the past 20 years.

"Everyone in our family knew it was his favourite possession. The piggy bank died with him," said Mrs Lau.

Mrs Lau and her daughter have since rented a place nearby to live - and she is worried about how she is going to afford a new house.

The government has said it will spend $867m (£663m) to acquire affected flats - but Mrs Lau says it is not nearly enough to buy a similarly sized flat in the area.

Still, her family was in a better position than many others, she said.

"Should I say that we are fortunate?

"I lost my husband but many families lost multiple family members... Babies less than a year old died. "

Stories have emerged of some of the other victims - a six-month-old who died alongside her 68-year-old grandmother when the fire broke out.

The bodies of an Indonesian domestic helper and the elderly person she worked for were found huddled together.

Image source, BBC Chinese / Phoebe Kong

Image caption,

Mrs Lau's son has since bought new piggy banks in memory of his father

As for Christy, she says she is planning to file a lawsuit against those responsible for the fire - but acknowledges that even if she wins, she "can't [get] my husband's life back".

"I share things that happen in our daily life, as if he still existed," she says. "I often write to him, 'I miss you so much. Are you doing well on the other side?'"

It's a similar story for Mrs Lau, who says she can't go anywhere without seeing her husband.

"Every day, something reminds me of him," she said.

"I still find it very hard to accept that my husband is gone, my home is gone, and so many of my neighbours are gone…. This place was my roots. I never imagined it would also mark an ending for me."

Moment Nasa spacecraft hit asteroid - and what happened next

Moment Nasa spacecraft hit asteroid - and what happened next

The first images of an asteroid that Nasa deliberately crashed into have revealed a stadium-sized crater on its surface.

Video released by Nasa showed the moment of impact in 2022, while new images show the extent of the damage done to the asteroid.

Dimorphos, the asteroid, posed no threat to Earth, but the crash was a test of our planetary defences to see if it was possible to knock a space rock off course.

Four years on, a European Space Agency (ESA) spacecraft called Hera is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision.

The BBC's science editor Rebecca Morelle explains.

items.title: Peter Magyar meets Volodymyr Zelenskyy: Hungary and Ukraine make a fresh start after the icy relations of the Viktor Orban era
items.summary: After years of frosty and hostile relations under Hungary's Kremlin-friendly former PM Viktor Orban, his successor, Peter Magyar, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy seek to reset their countries' ties.
items.body:
https://p.dw.com/p/5PtkN

Prefer DW on Google

Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar (left, pictured here with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy) said his visit to Ukraine marked the beginning of a new chapter in the relationship between Kyiv and BudapestImage: Genya Savilov/AFP

Advertisement

The location and the gesture were carefully chosen: Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stood side by side, laid flowers and bowed their heads at the military cemetery in the center of the Ukrainian city of Uzhhorod.

One of those buried there is an ethnic Hungarian who was one of the first soldiers killed in Russia's full-scale war of aggression against Ukraine.

Magyar intentionally chose not to begin his first visit to Ukraine as prime minister at a government building. Instead, his Tuesday afternoon visit began at a place where he could demonstrate his solidarity with Ukraine more clearly than anywhere else.

Uzhhorod, known as Ungvar in Hungarian, is the capital of Ukraine's Transcarpathia region, which is home to around 80,000 members of Ukraine's Hungarian minority. Thousands of ethnic Hungarians are fighting Russian occupying forces on the front lines.

For Hungary, where ethnic Hungarian minorities in neighboring countries traditionally play an important role, the war is therefore closer to home than it is for other European countries.

Magyar described his visit to Ukraine as a "historic day" in a Facebook post. Before the ceremony at the cemetery in Uzhhorod, he said: "I bring with me the solidarity of the Hungarian people. We stand with Ukraine against the Russian aggressor."

Zelenskyy responded on X, saying "We appreciate this gesture of respect toward those who sacrificed their lives for Ukraine's independence."

From low point to fresh start

The meeting between Magyar and Zelenskyy marked a turning point in Hungary's approach to Ukraine.

The two leaders repeatedly shook hands throughout the day. Such scenes would have been unthinkable just a few months ago. The propaganda of Magyar's pro-Russian predecessor, Viktor Orban, portrayed Ukraine as a "mafia state" and "lawless country" on an almost daily basis.

Under Orban, relations between Hungary and Ukraine reached a historic low.

Now the two countries are seeking a political reset, which is important not only for Hungary and Ukraine but for Europe as a whole. After all, Orban's repeated obstruction of support for Ukraine drove the EU to the brink of despair.

Closer economic cooperation

During talks in Uzhhorod, the two leaders also agreed to closer economic cooperation.

Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar (left) and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy laid wreaths and flowers at a ceremony commemorating the Ukrainian defenders who fell during the Russian invasionImage: Janos Nemes/MTI/AP Photo/picture alliance

The talks centered on Hungarian diesel supplies to Ukraine, greater use of Ukrainian gas storage facilities by Hungarian companies, and joint infrastructure projects, including the opening of new border crossings and a direct rail link between Budapest and Kyiv.

Nevertheless, no formal agreements were signed on Tuesday.

At a subsequent news conference, journalists asked questions about sensitive issues between the two countries: minority rights, Ukraine's EU integration and a new EU loan for Ukraine.

Throughout the day, the two men were visibly keen to avoid any discord.

Magyar, for example, described his angry outburst over Ukraine's "Carpathian Eight" initiative in parliament in late September as a "misunderstanding" and suggested that Hungary might, after all, take part.

Zelenskyy's cautious replies to journalists suggest that he knows his country's path to EU membership also runs through Budapest.

A fresh — but not always smooth — start

One of Magyar's statements on Tuesday was key: "We've finally put a stop to this completely unnecessary and inexplicable political escalation."

Even before taking office in early May 2026, Magyar had promised to reset relations with Ukraine. But the process has not been entirely smooth.

Posters belonging to Viktor Orban's Fidesz party portrayed Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Peter Magyar and Ursula von der Leyen as a risk and Fidesz as 'the better choice' in the run-up to the parliamentary election in AprilImage: Martin Fejer/estost.net/EST&OST/IMAGO

In many respects — but certainly not all — Magyar is distancing himself from his predecessor. He has made no bones of the fact that he sees Russia as the aggressor, but he rejects both arms deliveries to Ukraine and even the transit of weapons across Hungarian territory.

Magyar previously accused Ukraine of treating ethnic Hungarians as second-class citizens — a claim that is not borne out by the facts. He pressed for greater minority rights and for a time blocked the opening of negotiating chapters in Ukraine's EU accession talks.

Magyar also departed from diplomatic convention by choosing the location of his meeting with Zelenskyy in Ukraine: Indeed, it was Magyar who invited Zelenskyy to Transcarpathia.

Hungarian attitudes to Ukraine

Magyar's sometimes confrontational tone toward Ukraine can also be explained by the need to avoid appearing too pro-Ukrainian to the Hungarian public.

According to a November 2026 poll conducted by the think tank Globsec, 33% of Hungarians would now support their country providing military aid to Ukraine. Although this is much more than during Orban's time in office, many Hungarians remain skeptical of Ukraine.

items.summary: The first settlers of Liberia were African Americans who brought along the holiday of Thanksgiving — which has evolved to reflect the history and identity of this new nation.
items.body:
Global Health

How American Thanksgiving took root — and evolved — in Liberia

November 25, 20269:14 AM ET

Ari Daniel

Yvonne Capehart Weah's family routinely gets together in the township where she grew up in Liberia. In early November every year, they gather to celebrate the Liberian version of Thanksgiving.

Eddie Raynes

hide caption

Eddie Raynes

Yvonne Capehart Weah is from Liberia, a country in West Africa, and she's one of twelve siblings.

"I'm the second to the last one — I'm the eleventh," she says. "We have large families in Liberia."

Every year on the first Thursday in November, Weah's family gathers in Caldwell, the township where she grew up, to celebrate Liberian Thanksgiving.

"When we come together, the group become [so] large that you are not able to sit around a dining table," she explains. "So we do it outside under the tree. And when we meet, it's almost like we're having a party."

The Liberian holiday dates back to the first half of the 19th century when the American Colonization Society established the community that would grow into the country. It was founded by Black Americans — both those born free and enslaved people who had been emancipated — whose departure was sometimes voluntary, sometimes forced. "The settlers from America brought that Thanksgiving Day tradition to Liberia," says Weah. Once transplanted, the holiday evolved over time in response to national events.

Liberia gained its independence in 1847 but the British continued trying to take swaths of territory. In 1883, President Alfred Francis Russell, an Episcopalian priest, called upon God to help halt the incursions.

That invocation was a "prayer of protection against the intruders, preventing intrusion into our territory," says Weah.

The Liberians managed to maintain their sovereignty. And that year, the legislature officially established Thanksgiving as a national holiday steeped in the religious gratitude of the moment.

A sacred day for all

Weah summarizes Liberian Thanksgiving this way: "It's giving thanks to God for our freedom, for divine protection. It's giving thanks to God for unity and for the harvest."

Weah says that her family's celebration, like that of many others in Liberia, starts in the morning at church. But the holiday's for people of all faiths, and other religious communities mark the occasion as well

"The Muslims, they go to the mosques and pray," says Sekou Muhammad Sheriff, a YouTuber who travels his home country of Liberia to showcase its offerings and cultural heritage, including Thanksgiving. "And Muslims, Christians, and others — everybody observe this day as a holiday."

When Sheriff was a boy, this was the day that he counted on to get a new outfit.

"What my dad used to do for me," says Sheriff, was to purchase a "shirt-trouser suit, and then he'd buy me slipper." His favorite suit was a white one.

Over the years on Thanksgiving, he's grown accustomed to eating different stews, including one made with sweet potato leaves and another with snails collected from the garden.

"We call it king's meat," Sheriff says with a chuckle. "It is very, very nice."

The mid-afternoon meal varies from household to household in Liberia.

Yvonne Capehart Weah's nieces and nephews fill their plates at a family gathering in Caldwell.

Rebecca Blapoh Weah

hide caption

Rebecca Blapoh Weah

"We don't do turkey," says Weah, "but we do chicken. We do fried chicken, smoked chicken, roasted chicken."

Weah's family also serves jollof rice, watermelon, pineapple and a variety of stews, including one called fufu and soup. It's a mix of cassava, fish, chicken, okra, chili pepper and more. "That makes the soup very tasty," says Weah. "It has to be [at] every Thanksgiving."

(Weah doesn't especially like to cook, however. "If you tell me, 'Go in the kitchen to cook or sit in the living room and read,'" she says, "I will sit in the living room and read.")

"I'm thanking God"

This year, Sheriff didn't have the resources to host Thanksgiving. But he says that he remains thankful to God for keeping him healthy and for keeping Liberia peaceful after civil conflict tore his country apart from 1989 to 1997 and 1999 to 2003.

Weah is also grateful. "When I go for Thanksgiving," she says, "I'm thanking God for where I have come from, where I am now, and I'm also thanking Him for where He will take me because I know He holds the future."

Weah is the program manager at the We-Care Foundation, an education nonprofit that, among other things, teaches children literacy. "A reading child will become a reading elder," she says.

"And we expect informed adults to make informed decisions that affect both their social and economic life" — in ways, perhaps, that they will one day be thankful for.

Army to detonate tons of lead azide after delays. And, Abrego Garcia leaves U.S.

November 25, 20267:18 AM ET

By

Brittney Melton

Army Explosives Detonation In Iowa, Abrego Garcia Leaves The US, Congress And Nvidia

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

The Army will detonate a huge explosion in Middletown, Iowa, this morning to safely dispose of thousands of pounds of lead azide that could spontaneously explode. The explosive has been used since WWI and was moved to the Iowa bunker 17 years ago. The detonation is happening after officials found that the lead azide had crystallized and become unstable. Authorities have evacuated a 5-mile radius, and those within 20 miles are advised to stay indoors to avoid exposure to toxins.

A sign hangs from a fence surrounding the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, on Nov. 23, 2026, in Middletown, Iowa.

Scott Olson/Getty Images

hide caption

Scott Olson/Getty Images

• 🎧 The U.S. Army rescheduled the detonation multiple times after the public got wind of it last week, NPR's Quil Lawrence tells Up First. Purdue University's Andrew Whelton, who has worked on disaster planning, tells Lawrence the detonation caused stress for residents, businesses and farmers. The Trump administration pushed back on the notion that this planned action was a surprise, citing town hall meetings on the topic. Lawrence says the biggest danger in the detonation is to kids and pregnant people due to the lead dust in the air or on surfaces. There are also worries about potential harm to livestock and crops, as well as the cleanup duration.

Kilmar Abrego Garcia has voluntarily left the U.S. after a nearly two-year legal battle. He is the Salvadoran immigrant who became emblematic of the challenges posed by President Trump's mass deportation campaign. Abrego Garcia was arrested in 2025 and mistakenly deported to El Salvador. He returned to the U.S. but departed for Spain yesterday. His lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, said that Abrego Garcia boarded a commercial flight to a destination of his choice and "left the United States a free man." Sandoval-Moshenberg described the move as "a temporary departure," saying that Abrego Garcia, whose wife and child are U.S. citizens, has options to return to the U.S.

• 🎧 Abrego Garcia's attorney said that he will essentially spend two years waiting abroad. His case raises concerns about due process and the risks of sending individuals to countries where they could be harmed, NPR's Juliana Kim says. The Department of Homeland Security said they are delighted by his decision to leave the U.S. The agency, in a statement, said that "now this El Salvadoran man cannot terrorize innocents." After being mistakenly deported, upon his return to the U.S., Abrego Garcia was charged with human smuggling, an allegation he has denied.

Nvidia's newly reinstated CEO, Jensen Huang, apologized to his staff yesterday for his previous behavior, according to the New York Times. He reportedly denied that Trump pressured the board for his return, despite the president saying otherwise. Huang had stepped down following reports of affairs, including one with a woman reportedly suspected by U.S. intelligence agencies of being recruited by China's spy agency. Some members of Congress still have concerns about the national security scandal.

• 🎧 Some lawmakers are upset with Huang, while others criticized Nvidia and its board, NPR's Maham Javaid says. Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren says that Huang owes Congress answers about Nvidia's compliance with laws designed to keep advanced chips out of China. Republican Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas is calling for a congressional investigation into Huang and urging faster action on chip-control legislation. House Democratic Committee leaders sent a letter to the president after he claimed he helped with Huang's reinstatement. They asked if he prioritizes friends and allies over the nation's economic and national security interests. They demanded a response by Dec. 8 on what he knew about Huang's ties to an alleged Chinese spy. Huang will attend a closed-door hearing with House members next week, followed by testimony before a Senate committee two days later.

Today's listen

Tatyana Alanis for NPR

NPR launched the first-ever Senior Podcast Challenge this fall, inviting people over 65 to share their stories. Unlike the NPR Student Podcast Challenge, which has attracted more than 90,000 young voices since 2018, this contest focuses on the wisdom and experiences of older voices. While the contest is still open for a few more days, the judges have already listened to more than 100 submissions. Some stories explore life after retirement, dating after divorce or the loss of a partner, and coming to terms with being a senior. Take a listen to some of their favorite early entries.

There's still time to enter. The competition will close on Nov. 30. These are the official rules for the 2026 NPR Senior Podcast Challenge and you can submit your entry here.

Life advice

Beck Harlan for NPR

If you're spending your free time ruminating about work-related issues, you're essentially still on the clock, according to psychologist and author Guy Winch. Don't let workplace woes invade your home life. Winch shares techniques with Life Kit to help you reclaim your time, energy and attention when work consumes too much of your mental bandwidth.

• 🧠 Instead of reliving the work issue, spend 15 minutes creating a plan to address the situation. Ask yourself, "How can I handle this? What outcome do I want?"

• 🧠 Adopt rituals that engage as many senses as possible to help your brain transition between tasks. For example, try changing your clothes to signal the end of the workday. The more you repeat rituals, the easier it is for your brain to shift from work to relaxation.

• 🧠 Do something that energizes you. Activities like screen time and doomscrolling may seem relaxing, but they aren't effective.

• 🧠 Ask yourself: "If my job disappeared tomorrow, what remains of me?" You might realize your worth isn't tied to your job title.

For more guidance on how to switch off your work brain, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.

3 things to know before you go

Ezra Frech of Team United States competes during the Men's Long Jump T63 Final on three of the World Para Athletics Championships New Delhi 2025 at Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium on Sept. 29, 2025 in New Delhi, India.

Kenta Harada/Getty Images

hide caption

Kenta Harada/Getty Images

1. Dancing with the Stars wrapped up Season 35 last night, crowning Paralympian Ezra Frech and his partner, Daniella Karagach, as the winners of this year's Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy.

2. Frailejon, a plant of Colombia's high-mountain wetlands that's vital to the country's water supply, is facing an array of threats from farmers, ranchers and climate change. Volunteers are working to save these plants, one seedling at a time.

3. Doctors are combating disinformation about routine vitamin K shots for newborns, which prevent rare but life-threatening hemorrhaging. The rate of parents skipping these shots for their kids has increased from 3.1% in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025, according to new research in JAMA.

blocks.text: Nvidia's newly reinstated CEO, Jensen Huang, apologized to his staff yesterday for his previous behavior, according to the New York Times. He reportedly denied that Trump pressured the board for his return, despite the president saying otherwise. Huang had stepped down following reports of affairs, including one with a woman reportedly suspected by U.S. intelligence agencies of being recruited by China's spy agency. Some members of Congress still have concerns about the national security scandal.

items: 🎧 Some lawmakers are upset with Huang, while others criticized Nvidia and its board, NPR's Maham Javaid says. Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren says that Huang owes Congress answers about Nvidia's compliance with laws designed to keep advanced chips out of China. Republican Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas is calling for a congressional investigation into Huang and urging faster action on chip-control legislation. House Democratic Committee leaders sent a letter to the president after he claimed he helped with Huang's reinstatement. They asked if he prioritizes friends and allies over the nation's economic and national security interests. They demanded a response by Dec. 8 on what he knew about Huang's ties to an alleged Chinese spy. Huang will attend a closed-door hearing with House members next week, followed by testimony before a Senate committee two days later.

If you're spending your free time ruminating about work-related issues, you're essentially still on the clock, according to psychologist and author Guy Winch. Don't let workplace woes invade your home life. Winch shares techniques with Life Kit to help you reclaim your time, energy and attention when work consumes too much of your mental bandwidth.

items: 🧠 Instead of reliving the work issue, spend 15 minutes creating a plan to address the situation. Ask yourself, "How can I handle this? What outcome do I want?"

🧠 Adopt rituals that engage as many senses as possible to help your brain transition between tasks. For example, try changing your clothes to signal the end of the workday. The more you repeat rituals, the easier it is for your brain to shift from work to relaxation.
🧠 Do something that energizes you. Activities like screen time and doomscrolling may seem relaxing, but they aren't effective.
🧠 Ask yourself: "If my job disappeared tomorrow, what remains of me?" You might realize your worth isn't tied to your job title.
